body.text: In short:

The royal commission into Victoria's Big Build projects has heard the CFMEU promised construction company John Holland that it would be "looked at favourably" for future projects if it aligned itself with the union.
The hearing was told the exchange took place during a meeting in which the CFMEU put its demands to the company to lift a stop work on a Sunbury level crossing removal project.
The royal commission was earlier told of suspicions that the union had an alternative agenda when it raised dozens of safety concerns with the Sunbury project in one week.

The royal commission into Victoria's Big Build projects has heard a government minister's office had decided a major contractor would not win work on public sites if it did not give in to CFMEU demands.
The evidence emerged after two days of hearings examining a work stoppage at a level crossing removal project in Melbourne's north, which was contracted to the John Holland construction company.
In 2022, work ceased on the Gap Road project on June 6 and resumed on June 7 after control of the site was transferred to the CFMEU (Construction, Forestry, Mining and Energy Union).
The commission heard that project costs blew out by an estimated $6 million.
Today's hearing focused on dozens of incidents where CFMEU organisers raised safety concerns to gain entry to the Gap Road site, including 31 times on the week before the June 6 stoppage.
John Holland's general superintendent Steve Testolin told the royal commission he did not believe there were any valid safety issues on site and that he suspected the union had another agenda.
"April, May, there were continual requests to enter sites … it was more of an intelligence-gathering mission," Mr Testolin said.
He said the Gap Road site was the only level crossing removal project not aligned with the CFMEU.
He told the hearing about being summoned to a meeting at CFMEU's headquarters to receive the union's list of demands to resume work.
Mr Testolin said one of those present was senior CFMEU official Joe Myles.

"Joe then pretty much said, 'Enough with the small talk, what do you want?' and the room went pretty quiet and I just thought I'd just better say something so I said, 'How about you cut the bullshit and tell me what you want?'"

Mr Testolin told the hearing the union demanded John Holland employ a CFMEU-nominated health and safety representative, cease sourcing its workers through Zoom Recruitment and instead use the union's preferred BK Labour Hire, and also swap to CCL traffic management company.

He told the hearing he and the other John Holland representatives were then told that "if we aligned ourselves with the union than there'd be positive outcomes and we'd be looked at favourably for future projects".
When asked which projects the union was referring to, he answered: "Airport rail. We'd be one of the preferred contractors."
Mr Testolin told the royal commission that earlier in the day, John Holland had called WorkSafe and the police for help when negotiations with the CFMEU about the stoppage could not be resolved.
"WorkSafe was not prepared to come out immediately so at that point which was getting into the afternoon we requested police intervention.
"They were reluctant to come out as well, believing it was an [occupational health and safety] matter.
"As pressure and level crossings became more of a CFMEU-dominated area, we were being left to fend for ourselves."
Mr Testolin said John Holland also felt abandoned by the government representatives involved in the infrastructure project.
"Our safety records were above board but I knew that eventually we would have to concede [to aligning with the CFMEU] because we weren't being supported by authorities.
"We were pretty much being left standing alone."
Government office threatens John Holland joint venture
Joe Aygur accompanied Mr Testolin to the CFMEU meeting.
Mr Aygur was a manager with the Rail Network Alliance, a partnership between private companies and the government to deliver rail infrastructure.
He told the hearing he was on site on June 6 when the 24-hour operation came to a halt.
He said he was briefing Rail Projects Victoria (RPV) which is the government body responsible for the management of the state's major infrastructure projects.
Counsel assisting the royal commission, Chris Young KC asked Mr Aygur how he was being advised to fix the problem other than giving into the CFMEU's demands.
"That was the only approach," Mr Aygur answered.
Mr Aygur said RPV project director Peter Wilkinson told him to sit down with the CFMEU and resolve the issue.
"The intent of the words was there was a view in government that if we could not work through our industrial relations matters that we would not win further work in Victoria."
Under questioning, Mr Aygur said that Mr Wilkinson specified that that was the view of the minister's office.
Mr Aygur said at the time, the John Holland joint venture was actively vying for the Melbourne Airport project.
He then told the commission about a meeting with the CFMEU's Joe Myles and Paul Tzimas, which he said lasted roughly half a hour.
"The conversation started with Joe opening, words to the effect of 'So what have you got for me?'," Mr Aygur said.
"So there was an expectation that we were going there with some options.
"It soon then went across to Mr Tzimas where he gave a view of his view of how we were performing work within the alliance and it was a bit of an unpleasant view.

"He had raised his view that we as individuals or the alliance were not toeing the line, we were misbehaving, we were working in shutdown periods and lockdown periods, over long weekends and we were personally keeping him and his organisers away from family gatherings, birthdays, words to that effect and they had to come out on site to stop our work to keep us safe."
Dozens of disruptions by CFMEU before stop work

Earlier, crane operator Glenn Tyrrell told the royal commission he had been employed on the Gap Road project through Zoom Recruitment and was voted in by his colleagues as the site's health and safety representative during an election.

He said there was not much of a union presence at the Gap Road project until after April 2022 after which, at times, up to four CFMEU organisers would turn up and present John Holland site management with safety concerns.
"They'd just come on site and literally stop the whole job," Mr Tyrrell told the hearing.
"They'd have their [Right of Entry] paperwork and they'd stand in front of machinery and plant and just tell the operator that he must stop."
The commission heard that between May 25 and 31, the CFMEU issued 8 safety notices to John Holland.
It presented another 23 notices between June 1 and 2.
Mr Tyrrell described instances where union representatives would walk in front of cranes and even sat on concrete barriers that were about to be lifted into place to force the work to stop.
"Sometimes either the whole job site was shut or a certain area of the job was shut," Mr Tyrrell said.

He gave evidence that about a week after the June 6 stoppage, about 15 casual workers who had been hired through Zoom Recruitment were called into a lunch room and told they had to stop working for the labour hire firm and transfer to a new company, BK Labour Hire.
He said they were also told they were now required to join the CFMEU.
"That's the first time I joined any union," Mr Tyrrell told the hearing.
He said he had to make a bank transfer of $590 to the union up-front for half-yearly fees.
The hearing continues on Wednesday.
